labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Separating salt from sand
labs.aim: To separate a mixture of common salt and sand by dissolution, filtration and evaporation.
labs.theory: Salt is soluble in water while sand is not. Filtration removes the insoluble sand; evaporation removes the water, leaving salt behind.
labs.safety: Do not heat the china dish to complete dryness too fast — salt crystals may spatter.
procedure: Stir with glass rod and let it stand
Pour filtrate into china dish and heat
labs.result: Salt and sand are separated by dissolution, filtration and evaporation. Sand is obtained as residue; salt is recovered from the filtrate.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Soluble and insoluble substances
labs.aim: To classify substances as soluble or insoluble in water.
labs.theory: A substance that disappears uniformly in water is soluble. Insoluble solids settle; immiscible liquids form a separate layer.
procedure: Add a spoon of salt and shake
Add a spoon of sugar and shake
labs.result: Salt and sugar are soluble in water; sand is insoluble; oil is immiscible and floats on water.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Natural indicators: litmus, turmeric, china rose
labs.aim: To test acidic and basic substances using natural indicators.
labs.theory: Indicators change colour in acidic or basic media. Litmus: acid → red, base → blue. Turmeric: base → red-brown. China rose: acid → dark pink, base → green.
labs.result: Lemon juice is acidic and soap solution is basic, as shown by all three natural indicators.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Neutralisation of an acid by a base
labs.aim: To observe neutralisation of dilute HCl by NaOH using phenolphthalein.
labs.theory: An acid and a base react to form salt and water with release of heat. Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in base.
procedure: Add NaOH drop by drop until pink
Add one drop of dil. HCl
labs.result: Acid and base neutralise each other to form salt and water. The reaction is exothermic (temperature rose by ≈2.6 °C).

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Conditions necessary for rusting
labs.aim: To show that both air and water are needed for rusting of iron.
labs.theory: Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. Tube A has air and water; tube B has boiled water (no dissolved air) sealed by oil; tube C has dry air (CaCl₂ absorbs moisture).
labs.result: Iron rusts only when both air (oxygen) and water are present.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Crystallisation of copper sulphate
labs.aim: To obtain pure crystals of copper sulphate from an impure sample.
labs.theory: A hot saturated solution, on slow cooling, deposits pure crystals; impurities stay in solution. A few drops of dil. H₂SO₄ prevent hydrolysis.
procedure: Add CuSO₄ powder till no more dissolves
labs.result: Pure blue crystals of hydrated copper sulphate (CuSO₄·5H₂O) are obtained by crystallisation.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Oxides of metals and non-metals
labs.aim: To study the nature of oxides of magnesium (metal) and sulphur (non-metal).
labs.theory: Metal oxides are basic and turn red litmus blue; non-metal oxides are acidic and turn blue litmus red.
labs.safety: Do not look directly at burning magnesium. Burn sulphur only in a fume hood.
labs.result: Oxides of metals (MgO) are basic; oxides of non-metals (SO₂) are acidic.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Displacement: iron and copper sulphate
labs.aim: To show that iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution.
labs.theory: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution. Iron is more reactive than copper.
procedure: Dip a clean iron nail in CuSO₄
Dip a copper strip in FeSO₄
labs.result: Iron displaces copper from CuSO₄, but copper cannot displace iron. Iron is more reactive than copper.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Electrical conductivity of liquids
labs.aim: To test which liquids conduct electricity using a bulb-and-ammeter tester.
labs.theory: Solutions containing ions (electrolytes) conduct electricity. Strong electrolytes conduct well; weak ones poorly; non-electrolytes not at all.
labs.result: NaCl solution and dil. HCl are good conductors; vinegar and tap water conduct weakly; distilled water and sugar solution do not conduct.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Solution, suspension and colloid (Tyndall effect)
labs.aim: To distinguish true solution, suspension and colloid by appearance, stability and Tyndall effect.
labs.theory: Particles in a colloid (1–1000 nm) scatter light, making the beam path visible (Tyndall effect). Suspension particles are larger and settle.
procedure: Add a few drops of milk
Pass a torch beam through all
labs.result: Salt solution is a true solution; chalk in water is a suspension; milk in water is a colloid that shows the Tyndall effect and does not settle.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Melting point of ice & boiling point of water
labs.aim: To determine the melting point of ice and the boiling point of water.
labs.theory: During a change of state, heat supplied is used as latent heat, so temperature stays constant — at 0 °C while ice melts and at 100 °C while water boils (at 1 atm).
labs.safety: Do not let the thermometer bulb touch the bottom of the beaker.
procedure: Plot and interpret the heating curve.
labs.result: Melting point of ice = 0 °C. Boiling point of water = 100 °C. Temperature remains constant during both changes of state (latent heat).

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Mixture vs compound: iron and sulphur
labs.aim: To distinguish a mixture of iron filings and sulphur from the compound iron sulphide.
labs.theory: In a mixture, components retain their properties. On heating, iron and sulphur combine to form FeS, a new substance with different properties.
labs.safety: H₂S is toxic — perform in a fume hood.
labs.result: Iron and sulphur form a mixture before heating and the compound FeS after heating; the compound has properties different from its constituents.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Law of conservation of mass
labs.aim: To verify that mass is conserved in a chemical reaction.
labs.theory: In a closed system, the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products.
labs.result: Mass before and after the reaction is the same (152.36 g). Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Paper chromatography of ink
labs.aim: To separate the coloured components (dyes) of ink by paper chromatography.
labs.theory: Components travel with the solvent at different rates depending on solubility and adsorption on paper. Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent.
procedure: Place the strip in the solvent chamber.
Allow the solvent front to rise.
labs.result: Black ink is a mixture of blue, magenta and yellow dyes; green ink contains blue and yellow dyes. More soluble dyes travel further.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: pH of samples using universal indicator
labs.aim: To find the pH of various solutions using universal indicator and a pH meter.
labs.theory: pH = −log[H⁺]. pH < 7 acidic, = 7 neutral, > 7 basic. Universal indicator shows a colour for each pH value.
labs.result: Order of pH: HCl (1) < lemon juice (2.4) < ethanoic acid (3) < water (7) < NaHCO₃ (8.3) < NaOH (13).

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Properties of acids and bases
labs.aim: To study the reaction of HCl and NaOH with litmus, zinc and sodium carbonate.
labs.theory: Acids react with metals to release H₂ and with carbonates to release CO₂. CO₂ turns lime water milky; excess CO₂ clears it.
procedure: Pass the gas through lime water
labs.result: Acids turn blue litmus red, release H₂ with zinc and CO₂ with carbonates. Bases turn red litmus blue.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Types of chemical reactions
labs.aim: To study combination, decomposition, double displacement and precipitation reactions.
labs.theory: Combination: two substances form one. Decomposition: one substance breaks into simpler ones. Double displacement: exchange of ions, often forming a precipitate.
labs.result: CaO + water: combination (exothermic). FeSO₄ on heating: thermal decomposition. BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ and Pb(NO₃)₂ + KI: double displacement / precipitation.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Reactivity series of metals
labs.aim: To arrange Al, Zn, Fe and Cu in order of reactivity using displacement reactions.
labs.theory: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution.
labs.result: Order of reactivity: Al > Zn > Fe > Cu.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Soap in soft and hard water
labs.aim: To compare the foaming capacity of soap in soft and hard water.
labs.theory: Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺ ions in hard water react with soap to form insoluble scum, reducing lather. Detergents do not form scum.
procedure: Add soap to distilled water, shake
Add soap to hard water, shake
labs.result: Soap lathers well in soft water but forms scum in hard water. Detergents work in both.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Properties of ethanoic acid
labs.aim: To study odour, solubility, litmus test and reaction with NaHCO₃ of ethanoic acid.
labs.theory: Ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) is a weak acid, miscible with water, and reacts with carbonates to release CO₂.
labs.result: Ethanoic acid has a vinegar smell, is miscible with water, turns blue litmus red and liberates CO₂ with NaHCO₃.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Tests for anions
labs.aim: To identify CO₃²⁻, Cl⁻, SO₄²⁻ and NO₃⁻ ions in given salts.
labs.theory: Each anion gives a characteristic gas or precipitate with specific reagents.
labs.safety: Add conc. H₂SO₄ slowly along the side of the tube.
labs.result: Salt 1 contains CO₃²⁻, Salt 2 contains Cl⁻, Salt 3 contains SO₄²⁻ and Salt 4 contains NO₃⁻.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Tests for cations
labs.aim: To identify Cu²⁺, Fe³⁺, Pb²⁺ and Zn²⁺ ions by confirmatory tests.
labs.theory: Cations form characteristic coloured precipitates or complexes with group reagents.
labs.result: Cu²⁺: deep blue with excess NH₄OH. Fe³⁺: Prussian blue / blood red. Pb²⁺: yellow PbI₂. Zn²⁺: white ppt soluble in excess NaOH.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Flame test for metal ions
labs.aim: To identify metal ions by the colour they impart to a non-luminous flame.
labs.theory: Heat excites electrons; as they return to lower levels they emit light of characteristic wavelengths.
labs.safety: Clean the wire in conc. HCl between tests.
labs.result: Na⁺ golden yellow, K⁺ lilac, Ca²⁺ brick red, Sr²⁺ crimson, Ba²⁺ apple green, Cu²⁺ bluish green.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Titration: NaOH vs standard oxalic acid
labs.aim: To determine the molarity of NaOH by titrating it against 0.05 M oxalic acid.
labs.theory: At the end point, moles of NaOH = 2 × moles of oxalic acid. Phenolphthalein turns from colourless to pink at pH ≈ 8.2.
labs.safety: Read the lower meniscus at eye level. Remove the funnel before titrating.
procedure: Transfer the measured sample to the flask.
Titrate slowly to the end point.
Repeat until concordant readings are obtained.
labs.result: Molarity and strength of NaOH are calculated from the concordant titre value.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Titration: Na₂CO₃ vs HCl (methyl orange)
labs.aim: To determine the molarity of Na₂CO₃ solution using 0.1 M HCl.
labs.theory: Na₂CO₃ reacts with HCl in 1:2 ratio. Methyl orange changes from yellow (basic) to orange-red (acidic) at pH ≈ 3.1–4.4.
procedure: Transfer the measured sample to the flask.
Titrate slowly to the end point.
Repeat until concordant readings are obtained.
labs.result: Molarity and strength of Na₂CO₃ are calculated from the concordant titre value.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Redox titration: KMnO₄ vs oxalic acid
labs.aim: To determine the molarity of KMnO₄ using standard 0.05 M oxalic acid.
labs.theory: KMnO₄ acts as a self-indicator. The reaction is slow at room temperature and is carried out at 60–70 °C in acid medium.
labs.safety: Read the upper meniscus for coloured KMnO₄.
procedure: Transfer the measured sample to the flask.
Titrate slowly to the end point.
Repeat until concordant readings are obtained.
labs.result: Molarity and strength of KMnO₄ are calculated from the concordant titre value.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Redox titration: KMnO₄ vs Mohr’s salt
labs.aim: To determine the molarity of KMnO₄ using standard 0.1 M Mohr’s salt solution.
labs.theory: Fe²⁺ is oxidised to Fe³⁺ by MnO₄⁻ in acid medium at room temperature. KMnO₄ is the self-indicator.
procedure: Transfer the measured sample to the flask.
Titrate slowly to the end point.
Repeat until concordant readings are obtained.
labs.result: Molarity and strength of KMnO₄ are calculated from the concordant titre value.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Chromatography of leaf pigments
labs.aim: To separate pigments from spinach leaf extract by paper chromatography and find their Rf values.
labs.theory: Pigments differ in solubility in the non-polar solvent and adsorption on cellulose. Carotene (least polar) moves farthest.
procedure: Place the strip in the solvent chamber.
Allow the solvent front to rise.
labs.result: Four pigments separate: β-carotene (orange, Rf ≈ 0.94), xanthophyll (yellow, 0.71), chlorophyll a (blue-green, 0.47), chlorophyll b (yellow-green, 0.34).

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Enthalpy of neutralisation
labs.aim: To determine the enthalpy of neutralisation of HCl with NaOH.
labs.theory: Heat released = m·c·ΔT. For a strong acid–strong base, ΔH ≈ −57 kJ mol⁻¹.
procedure: Pour NaOH into calorimeter and stir
labs.result: Enthalpy of neutralisation of HCl by NaOH ≈ −56 kJ mol⁻¹ (literature −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹).

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Shift in chemical equilibrium
labs.aim: To study the shift in equilibrium by changing concentration of ions (Le Chatelier’s principle).
labs.theory: Adding a reactant shifts equilibrium forward; the colour of the product deepens. Diluting shifts the cobalt equilibrium back to the pink aqua complex.
labs.result: Increasing concentration of a reactant shifts equilibrium in the forward direction; dilution shifts the cobalt equilibrium backward, as predicted by Le Chatelier’s principle.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Rate of reaction: concentration & temperature
labs.aim: To study the effect of concentration and temperature on the rate of reaction between Na₂S₂O₃ and HCl.
labs.theory: Colloidal sulphur makes the solution turbid. Time t for a cross mark to disappear is inversely related to rate. Rate rises with concentration; roughly doubles per 10 °C rise.
procedure: Stop when the visual end point is reached.
labs.result: Time for the cross to disappear decreases as concentration or temperature increases — the rate (∝ 1/t) increases.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Tests for functional groups
labs.aim: To identify unsaturation, alcoholic, phenolic, aldehydic, carboxylic and amino groups.
labs.theory: Each functional group gives a characteristic colour, precipitate or gas with specific reagents.
labs.result: Sample tests confirm: C=C (bromine water), –OH alcohol (CAN), phenol (FeCl₃), aldehyde (Tollens’, Fehling’s), –COOH (NaHCO₃), aromatic amine (azo dye test).

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Tests for carbohydrates, proteins and fats
labs.aim: To detect carbohydrates, proteins and oils/fats in given food samples.
labs.theory: Iodine gives blue-black with starch; reducing sugars reduce Fehling’s to Cu₂O; peptide bonds give violet with biuret reagent; Molisch gives a violet ring with carbohydrates.
labs.result: Starch, reducing sugar, protein, carbohydrate and oil were identified by iodine, Fehling’s, biuret, Molisch and acrolein tests respectively.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Variation of cell EMF (Daniell cell)
labs.aim: To study the variation of EMF of the Zn|Zn²⁺||Cu²⁺|Cu cell with change in electrolyte concentration.
labs.theory: By the Nernst equation, EMF decreases as [Cu²⁺] decreases and increases as [Zn²⁺] decreases. E° = 1.10 V.
labs.result: EMF decreases with decrease in [Cu²⁺] and increases with decrease in [Zn²⁺], in agreement with the Nernst equation.

labs.subject: chemistry
labs.title: Lyophilic and lyophobic sols
labs.aim: To prepare starch sol (lyophilic) and ferric hydroxide sol (lyophobic).
labs.theory: Lyophilic sols form directly on mixing. Lyophobic sols need special methods — Fe(OH)₃ sol forms by hydrolysis of FeCl₃ in boiling water.
labs.result: Starch sol (lyophilic) and ferric hydroxide sol (lyophobic) were prepared; both show the Tyndall effect.
